analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and pays for it with taxes on high incomes and investments.
analysis.headline: A bill to expand Social Security and fund it with new taxes on incomes above $250,000 and investment gains never got a hearing in committee and died at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security checks: a bigger across-the-board increase, cost-of-living adjustments tied to the inflation seniors actually experience, a higher minimum benefit for low lifetime earners, and longer benefits for students whose parent is retired, disabled, or deceased. To pay for it, it applies the Social Security payroll tax to wages above $250,000 (currently capped around $160,000), applies payroll tax to large pass-through business income, raises the tax on net investment income from 3.8% to 16.2%, and merges the retirement and disability trust funds into one. It was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries: roughly a bigger benefit for retirees and disabled workers (larger bend-point percentage and a 22% adjustment to the benefit formula), seniors whose COLA would track the CPI for Elderly Consumers rather than the general CPI, lifetime low earners whose new minimum benefit rises toward 125% of the federal poverty line with years of work, and children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers who could keep benefits through age 22 as full-time students. Higher earners above $250,000 and large investment income earners would pay more taxes that fund these increases and extend the program's solvency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries, especially low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the first bend-point percentage from 90% to 95% and adds a 22% adjustment to the bend-point amount, increasing benefits for all current and future beneficiaries.
Replaces the standard Consumer Price Index with the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers (CPI-E) for annual cost-of-living adjustments, better reflecting what seniors actually buy.

Establishes a new minimum benefit scaled to years in the workforce, rising to 125% of the federal poverty line for those with 30 or more years of work, protecting lifetime low earners from poverty in old age.
Extends benefits to children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers until age 22 if they are full-time students, up from the current age-19/secondary-school cutoff.

Applies the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $250,000 (the 2023 cap was $160,200) and raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2%, extending the program's solvency for decades.
Merges the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Disability Insurance trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund.

analysis.who_pays: High earners: wages above $250,000 become subject to the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax for workers and employers; owners of pass-through businesses would see that income subject to payroll tax through the expanded net investment income tax; and all net investment income would face a 16.2% tax (up from 3.8%). Wealthy households with large investment portfolios bear the largest share.

drawbacks.text: The 16.2% tax on net investment income is a substantial increase from the current 3.8% and could reduce incentives for investment, affecting markets and retirement portfolios held broadly by middle-class households as well.

Applying payroll tax above $250,000 without crediting benefits for that income (the bill's text changes the tax base without a corresponding benefit formula change) means very high earners pay in more relative to what they receive back, a form of benefit-cut for the top of the income distribution that some argue breaks the program's earned-benefit framing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit increases are broad and immediate while the taxes are concentrated at the very top of the income and wealth distribution. The main honest trade-off is that the investment-income tax increase is large and would touch broad retirement accounts indirectly, and the payroll tax extension means top earners pay more without proportional benefit credits. On net, the bill shifts resources to lower- and middle-income seniors and their dependents, financed by the highest earners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee—referred to three committees on introduction and later to a Social Security subcommittee—and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced February 14, 2023 by Rep. Schakowsky with 26 original cosponsors.
Referred to the House Committees on Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Transportation and Infrastructure on the day of introduction.
Grew to 37 cosponsors, all Democrats, over the life of the bill.
Referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security on December 17, 2024, over 21 months after introduction.
No hearings, markups, or floor votes occurred; the Congress ended January 3, 2025 without action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and investors are better off because the bill never advanced: the new payroll tax above $250,000 and the 16.2% investment-income tax never materialized. Current beneficiaries are not worse off, but they also did not get the proposed benefit increases, and the program's long-term financing shortfall remains unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors; no one else changed materially

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 26 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 37 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Referral committee holding jurisdiction over Social Security financing
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the 118th Congress; the bill was instead referred to a subcommittee in the final weeks of 2024.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling House floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor at any point in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were House Democrats; the Republican majority controlled scheduling and no floor action ever occurred.

industries.note: Would face a new 12.4% payroll tax on wages above $250,000. Opposing the bill preserved the current cap around $160,000.

industries.industry: Owners of investment income and pass-through business income
industries.note: Net investment income tax would have risen from 3.8% to 16.2% and covered active business income. The bill's defeat preserved the lower rate and narrower base.
